meaning: application or request; the physical form may be called formulario de solicitud.
category: contact-related semantic extension; feminine noun.
region: DPD aplicar(se), §2: much of America; no current frequency estimate.
example: Recibimos tu aplicación ayer. — We received your application yesterday.
guidance: The extension names a request. Do not assume every institution uses it for a blank application form.

meaning: apply for a job or another opportunity.
category: contact-related semantic and syntactic extension; verb.
region: DPD aplicar(se), §2: normal in much of America; audience and institutional register matter.
example: Voy a aplicar para ese puesto. — I'm going to apply for that position.
guidance: A plan is not a submitted application. Presentar una solicitud is a useful alternative, without condemning a documented variety.

meaning: chat using an online chat service.
category: established Spanish verb formed from English to chat and -ear.
region: DLE chatear²; general dictionary entry, without a U.S.-only claim.
example: Estamos chateando sobre el archivo. — We're chatting online about the file.
guidance: The sense and English source are documented. This does not turn every use into a language switch.

meaning: check or compare in the selected reviewing sense.
category: adapted English-derived Spanish verb, from to check.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S., Mexico and specified other American areas; popular register, Ecuador marked less used.
example: Voy a checar la lista. — I'm going to check the list.
guidance: Select a sense; other meanings include marking a check and clocking in. Do not equate every English check expression with this verb.

meaning: check or review in sense I.1.
category: adapted English-derived Spanish verb, from to check.
region: ASALE I.1 includes U.S. and numerous American countries; further senses have separate geographical labels.
example: Ya chequeé los nombres. — I already checked the names.
guidance: The checking sense does not automatically cover every registration, baggage or social use listed elsewhere under the lemma.

meaning: send something by fax.
category: Spanish verb formed on the English-derived noun fax.
region: DPD fax, §1; no claim about present-day prevalence.
example: ¿Puedes faxear el formulario? — Can you fax the form?
guidance: Also printed in Cruz–Teck (1998), p. 87. The medium may be needed in some settings; an older attestation alone does not make the word obsolete.

meaning: guard or watchman in the selected sense.
category: watchman-derived adapted noun; ASALE labels its origin calco.
region: ASALE I.1 lists Mexico, much of Central America, the Dominican Republic and several South American countries; popular/spontaneous use.
example: Hablemos con el guachimán. — Let's speak with the guard.
guidance: The source's etymological label is retained here. In this book's form-versus-meaning analysis it illustrates adaptation of English material, rather than a word-for-word translation into existing Spanish words.

meaning: guard or watchman.
category: watchman-derived adapted noun; source-specific variant.
region: ASALE I.1: Puerto Rico; compare the linked guachimán entry.
example: El guáchiman vigila la entrada. — The guard watches the entrance.
guidance: The written accent distinguishes the documented stress pattern. Do not apply the Puerto Rican label automatically to every spelling variant.

meaning: go out for fun.
category: documented variant linked to janguear.
region: ASALE I.1: Puerto Rico; spontaneous socializing sense.
example: ¿Van a hanguear el sábado? — Are they going out Saturday?
guidance: This is a reference variant, not an instruction to change the characters' accent.

meaning: socialize, go out for enjoyment; selected senses vary.
category: adapted English-derived Spanish verb, from to hang (around).
region: ASALE I.1: U.S., popular; I.2: Puerto Rico, spontaneous popular/educated use.
example: ¿Quieres janguear el sábado? — Want to hang out Saturday?
guidance: These senses concern social activity or being unoccupied, not hanging a picture on a wall. Region labels do not compel anyone to use it.

meaning: relaxed socializing with companions, conversation or jokes.
category: related Spanish noun in the contact-derived lexical family.
region: ASALE I.1: Puerto Rico; popular/educated spontaneous use; no U.S. label in this entry.
example: Un jangueo tranquilo en el café. — A relaxed hangout at the café.
guidance: A noun and its related verb can have different dictionary distributions. Do not copy the verb's labels into this entry.

meaning: janguear in the sense selected by context.
category: documented variant linked to janguear.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S. and Puerto Rico.
example: No puedo janguiar esta noche. — I can't hang out tonight.
guidance: A linked variant documents that spelling; it does not license unlimited respelling.

meaning: light midday meal in sense I.1.
category: adapted English-derived masculine noun, from lunch.
region: ASALE I.1 includes U.S., Mexico and specified other areas; Puerto Rico marked less used. Afternoon and miner's-meal senses have different labels.
example: Traje un lonche para el viaje. — I brought a light meal for the trip.
guidance: Food and its container are different referents. Do not infer an English midday meaning for every regional sense.

meaning: eat a lonche or have a light meal in the documented senses.
category: regional Spanish verb related to the English-derived noun lonche.
region: ASALE I.1: Mexico, Nicaragua; Ecuador popular. I.2: transitive use in Mexico.
example: Vamos a lonchear al mediodía. — Let's have lunch at noon.
guidance: The cited entry does not give a U.S. tag. Related forms need separate documentation.

meaning: lunch box; portable container for food.
category: documented Spanish noun in the lunch-related lexical family.
region: ASALE I.1 includes U.S. and many American countries and highlights use by schoolchildren.
example: La lonchera está vacía. — The lunch box is empty.
guidance: The fictional adult use is an authored situation; this entry does not establish its frequency in a particular Texas household.

meaning: park a vehicle in sense I.1.
category: adapted English-derived Spanish verb, from to park.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S., northern Mexico and numerous American areas; other senses and pronominal uses have their own labels.
example: ¿Ya parqueaste la troca? — Have you parked the truck yet?
guidance: Parqueé and parqueaste have Spanish person/tense endings. Estacionar is an alternative, not a universal correction.

meaning: print using a printer.
category: adapted English-derived Spanish verb, from to print.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S., El Salvador, Puerto Rico; Ecuador marked less used.
example: Voy a printear las páginas aprobadas. — I'll print the approved pages.
guidance: Cruz–Teck (1998), printed p. 87, PDF p. 89, is historical attestation. Neither source establishes its prevalence in every office today.

meaning: report or communicate information to someone.
category: documented English-influenced Spanish verb; selected communication sense.
region: ASALE I.3 includes U.S. and specified American countries; other reporting or pronominal senses differ.
example: Voy a reportar el error. — I'm going to report the error.
guidance: The plan does not establish that a report has been made or a problem repaired. Reportarse has additional meanings; consult the relevant sense.

meaning: restart in the computing sense; specify the intended operation.
category: established Spanish verb formed from English to reset and -ear.
region: DLE resetear, computing sense; no claim of a special regional distribution.
example: Antes de resetear el equipo, aclaremos qué hace falta. — Before resetting the device, let's clarify what's needed.
guidance: Reset is not a safe universal instruction: distinguish restarting from restoring settings or erasing data in the particular context.

meaning: roof of a building.
category: adapted English-derived masculine noun, from roof.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S.; the entry gives no current frequency measure.
example: El rufo necesita reparación. — The roof needs repairs.
guidance: A U.S. record does not establish Miami-only use. Ask which roof or part of it when the task needs precision.

meaning: sweater.
category: established adapted Spanish loan, from sweater.
region: DLE, masculine noun; no U.S.-only label.
example: Los suéteres azules están listos. — The blue sweaters are ready.
guidance: The Spanish plural and adjective agreement are ordinary Spanish grammar; English origin does not make each occurrence a switch.

meaning: cargo truck or pickup in separately recorded senses.
category: adapted English-derived feminine noun, from truck.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S. Southwest, northern Mexico, Nicaragua, cargo truck; I.2: El Salvador, pickup.
example: La troca está afuera. — The truck is outside.
guidance: Do not infer one vehicle model from the lemma alone. Its unrelated Peruvian sense is outside this course's transport example.

meaning: yard or garden area belonging to a building.
category: English-derived feminine noun in the selected yard sense.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S. Southwest, northern Honduras, Panama.
example: Hay herramientas en la yarda. — There are tools in the yard.
guidance: This sense is distinct from the unit of length. A shared spelling does not establish a shared referent.

meaning: vehicle salvage yard or junkyard.
category: adapted English-derived masculine noun; source etymon junker.
region: ASALE I.1: U.S. Southwest and Mexico.
example: Busquemos la pieza en el yonque. — Let's look for the part at the salvage yard.
guidance: The source supports the selected sense and labels, not the existence of a particular business or present-day frequency.

meaning: in a moment/later; now or a recent past in other listed senses.
category: regional Spanish time adverb; no English origin asserted.
region: ASALE I.1 includes the U.S. and many American regions for a near future; I.2 lists a recent past with distinct labels; I.3 lists Venezuela, Ecuador and Bolivia for present time.
example: ¿Nos vemos ahorita? — Shall we meet in a little while? (provisional contextual reading).
guidance: Confirm an agreed time when precision matters; the translation is not a universal fixed-minute definition.

meaning: a lively group of young people in the selected sense.
category: regional Spanish masculine noun; no English derivation asserted.
region: ASALE I.1: Puerto Rico; popular/educated spontaneous use.
example: El corillo llegó temprano. — The group arrived early.
guidance: The source's youth-related meaning is narrower than a universal word for friends. No claim is made about every U.S. Latino community.

meaning: bus in the selected transport sense; baby or child in separately recorded senses.
category: regional polysemy; no English derivation asserted here.
region: ASALE II.1: northwestern Mexico, western Guatemala, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico; II.2: larger passenger vehicle in Puerto Rico. Child senses I.1–2 have different American labels.
example: ¿A qué hora pasa la guagua? — What time does the bus come by? (transport context).
guidance: Do not assign a speaker's origin from the noun or file every sense under a single etymology.

meaning: close friend or companion in the selected sense.
category: regional polysemous noun; no English derivation asserted here.
region: ASALE I.1 includes U.S., Mexico, Panama, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Venezuela, Ecuador, western Bolivia and additional youth-register records.
example: Gracias por venir, pana. — Thanks for coming, buddy.
guidance: Other senses include a breakdown or breadfruit in their specified regions. Familiar address needs relationship and context.
